lead: Prestressed concrete squeezes the concrete before the load arrives. A stretched high-strength steel tendon pulls back on the ends of the beam and puts the whole section into compression. Bending from load then has to eat through that compression before any tension appears, so cracks start much later, or never. The same trick lets a beam be shallower and span farther than ordinary reinforced concrete. You meet it in long bridge girders, thin floor slabs, water tanks, pipes, railway sleepers and precast roof units across India.
prereq: You need: concrete properties and characteristic strength from Unit 1, the simple bending stress f = My/I from Unit 2, and a first look at high-strength steel from 6.2.

blocks.text: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension. A plain concrete beam cracks when the bending tension reaches roughly one-tenth of its compressive strength. Ordinary reinforced concrete accepts this: the concrete cracks, and steel bars inside carry the tension that the concrete cannot.
Prestressing reverses the order. Before the load comes, the concrete is deliberately put into compression. Later bending tension must first cancel that compression before it can crack anything.

The force comes from a tendon: a cable of high-strength steel wires, strands or bars, stretched by a hydraulic jack. The jacking force P, in kN or N, is the force in the tendon at the moment the jack stretches it.

When the jack is released, the tendon tries to shrink back. Its ends are held by anchorages bearing on the concrete, so it drags the concrete with it and the section is squeezed. That hand-over of force from jack to concrete is called transfer. The force left after transfer is smaller than P; the losses are covered in 6.5.

Where the tendon sits matters. The eccentricity e is the distance from the centroidal axis of the section to the tendon, in mm. The tendon pulls with P at depth e; the concrete pushes back with P along the axis; the two form a couple that resists bending. That is the internal couple of a prestressed member.

blocks.where: M<sub>r</sub> is the moment resisted by the prestress couple, in N·mm; P is the tendon force in N; e is the eccentricity in mm, measured from the centroidal axis to the tendon.

sections.h3: Adding the stresses: decompression and cracking

blocks.text: At any fibre, the stress is the sum of three parts: the axial squeeze P/A, the bending P·e·y/I caused by the eccentric tendon, and the bending M·y/I from the applied load. Take compression as positive throughout.

blocks.where: f is the stress at the fibre in N/mm²; P the tendon force in N; A the concrete area in mm²; e the eccentricity in mm; y the distance from the centroidal axis to the fibre in mm; I the second moment of area in mm⁴; M the applied bending moment in N·mm. Choose each sign by looking at the fibre: a tendon below the axis adds compression at the bottom and takes it away at the top.

blocks.text: As load grows, the stress at the tension face falls. The load at which that stress just becomes zero is the decompression load. Beyond it, tension starts to build; the concrete cracks only when that tension reaches its own tensile strength. So the whole range from zero load to cracking stays uncracked, and an uncracked section is stiff and barely deflects.

The couple P × e already acts as a built-in hogging moment before any load arrives. This is why a prestressed beam usually bows upward, a camber, when it is taken off the bed. Choosing a tendon profile so that this upward effect cancels part of the downward load is the load-balancing idea of 6.4.

items: Smaller, lighter sections for the same span, which cuts dead load and foundation cost.
Longer spans are possible: a prestressed girder can cross a gap that would need a much deeper reinforced concrete girder.
The section stays uncracked under service load, which suits water tanks, pipes and other liquid-retaining structures.
High-strength steel is used efficiently, close to its design strength, because crack width does not limit it the way it limits ordinary rebar (see 6.2).
Factory precasting gives good control, quick erection and less site labour: bridge girders, sleepers, electric poles and floor units are common examples.
Camber under prestress offsets part of the later sag, so deflections stay small.

blocks.text: The cost is skill and hardware: jacks, anchorages, ducts, high-strength steel, and a strong concrete mix. A heavy force enters at a small anchorage and spreads out, so the end block needs its own reinforcement (6.7). For short spans and light loads, ordinary reinforced concrete is still cheaper.

figure.caption: The jack stretches the tendon and transfer squeezes the concrete; the later load then cancels part of that compression, so cracking is pushed to a higher load.

spec.title: How prestress works
spec.aria: A stretched tendon pre-compresses the concrete, and later load cancels part of the bending tension so cracking is delayed.

examples.question: A rectangular beam 200 mm wide and 400 mm deep carries a straight tendon with jacking force P = 400 kN. (a) Find the stress when the tendon is concentric. (b) Find the top and bottom fibre stresses when the tendon is placed 100 mm below the centroidal axis. (c) For that eccentric tendon, a sagging moment later causes 8 N/mm² bending tension at the bottom fibre — find the net bottom stress, and compare with the concentric case.
steps: Area of the section: A = 200 × 400 = 80,000 mm².
Concentric tendon: f = P/A = 400,000 / 80,000 = 5 N/mm² compression, uniform over the section.
Second moment of area: I = b·D³/12 = 200 × 400³ / 12 = 1.0667 × 10⁹ mm⁴; distance to the extreme fibre y = 400/2 = 200 mm.
Prestress bending from eccentricity: P·e·y/I = 400,000 × 100 × 200 / (1.0667 × 10⁹) = 8 × 10⁹ / (1.0667 × 10⁹) = 7.5 N/mm².
Top fibre: 5 − 7.5 = −2.5, that is 2.5 N/mm² tension, present even before any load.
Apply the load: bottom stress = 8 − 12.5 = −4.5, so 4.5 N/mm² compression; the bottom never goes into tension.
Concentric comparison: bottom stress = 8 − 5 = 3 N/mm² tension, so the concentric beam would crack while the eccentric one does not.
examples.answer: Concentric prestress gives 5 N/mm² compression everywhere; the tendon at e = 100 mm gives 12.5 N/mm² compression at the bottom and 2.5 N/mm² tension at the top, so under the 8 N/mm² load the bottom stays 4.5 N/mm² in compression instead of 3 N/mm² in tension.
examples.check:
b, D, P, e = 200.0, 400.0, 400e3, 100.0
A = b * D
f_axial = P / A
I = b * D**3 / 12
y = D / 2
f_bend = P * e * y / I
f_bottom = f_axial + f_bend
f_top_tension = f_bend - f_axial
f_load = 8.0
net_bottom_comp = f_bottom - f_load
net_concentric_tension = f_load - f_axial
print(round(f_axial, 4))
print(round(f_bend, 4))
print(round(f_bottom, 4))
print(round(f_top_tension, 4))
print(round(net_bottom_comp, 4))
print(round(net_concentric_tension, 4))

traps: Prestress does not make concrete strong in tension. It only adds compression; if the load's tension exceeds the pre-compression plus the concrete's own tensile strength, the section still cracks and must be checked.

Sign slips. With compression positive, a tendon below the axis adds compression at the bottom and reduces it at the top, which can leave the top in tension under prestress alone. Always draw the stress diagram at top and bottom.
The jacking force is not the force that stays in the tendon. Transfer, friction, anchorage slip, creep, shrinkage and relaxation all reduce it (see 6.5). Design with the effective force.
Eccentricity e is measured from the centroidal axis, never from the top or bottom face. Measuring from the face gives a wrong P·e·y/I and wrong stresses.
Prestressing is not the same thing as using high-strength concrete. Strong concrete is needed because the prestress is large, but the tensile force is carried by the tendon.

quiz.q: Define tendon, jacking force and transfer.
quiz.a: A tendon is a high-strength steel wire, strand or bar cable that carries the prestressing force. The jacking force P is the force in the tendon while the jack stretches it. Transfer is the hand-over of that force from the jack to the concrete through the anchorages.

quiz.q: What is the eccentricity of a tendon?
quiz.a: The perpendicular distance from the centroidal axis of the concrete section to the tendon, in mm.

quiz.q: Why does a prestressed beam stay uncracked at a load where a similar reinforced concrete beam has already cracked?
quiz.a: The tendon has already put the concrete into compression. The bending tension from load must first cancel that compression (decompression) before any tensile stress appears in the concrete. In reinforced concrete the steel is passive, so the concrete takes the whole tension and cracks early.

quiz.q: Explain the internal couple P × e in a prestressed beam.
quiz.a: The tendon pulls with force P at depth e below the centroidal axis, and the concrete pushes back with P along the axis. These two equal and opposite forces form a couple of magnitude P × e that resists the applied bending moment and produces camber.

quiz.q: A 150 mm × 300 mm section carries a concentric tendon force of 300 kN. Find the uniform stress.
For the same 150 mm × 300 mm section, the 300 kN tendon is moved 75 mm below the centroidal axis. Find the top and bottom fibre stresses.

A beam is prestressed concentrically and, at service load, the bottom fibre stress is exactly zero. The tendon is then shifted 50 mm downward. What changes at the two faces, and which face now controls cracking?
quiz.a: The centroidal axis and P/A are unchanged, but the P·e·y/I term appears: bottom gains compression, top loses it. The bottom now has a margin against cracking and the decompression load there rises. The top, already reduced, may go into tension under the prestress alone, so the top fibre now controls cracking and the section may crack there even before full load.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern practice adds external tendons, placed outside the concrete and deflectable, so they can be inspected and replaced, and unbonded tendons with greased strands for slabs. Fibre-reinforced polymer tendons resist corrosion in coastal bridges. Load balancing, introduced by T. Y. Lin, is now the usual way of choosing tendon profiles. Good search words: external prestressing, load balancing method, unbonded tendons, the Indian code for prestressed concrete.
